steps.title: A map, not a build
steps.body: A Zmod pod plugs into a SYZYGY port. The port is wired to the FPGA, so the processors cannot reach the ADC until a design in the fabric provides a controller for it and Linux has a driver for that controller. The row at the bottom is the order in which to do the work.

steps.title: The pod and its port
steps.body:
A Zmod Scope is a two-channel, 14-bit, 100 MS/s ADC board. It plugs into SYZYGY port A or B, each wired to its own bank of fabric I/O and not to the processors. A small microcontroller on the board reads the pod's identity over I2C and sets the port's supply voltage first.

Pods are not hot-swappable: power the board off before you plug or unplug one.

steps.title: The design in the fabric
steps.body: Digilent publishes IP for each Zmod: a controller with AXI-Lite registers and a stream output, plus a standard AXI DMA that moves the stream into DDR. You instantiate them in Vivado with the board's PS preset and produce a bitstream. Nothing of it exists until the bitstream is loaded.

steps.title: The way samples reach the PS
steps.body: Registers are read through a general-purpose port; the DMA writes samples to memory through a high-performance port; completion interrupts arrive on `IRQ_F2P` lines, which the device tree must name by number.

steps.title: The driver
steps.body: The kernel already has `xilinx_dma` for the DMA engine. The ADC controller needs its own driver (an IIO driver, or Digilent's UIO plus `xilinx_axidma` approach), and a device-tree node with the addresses and interrupt numbers from the Vivado export.

steps.title: Step 1: get the PS working first
steps.body: Everything in this repository. If the board boots, has a console and Ethernet, any later problem is in the PL design or the driver, not in the boot chain.

steps.title: Step 2: build the PL design
steps.body: In Vivado, outside this repository. Start from the board preset and Digilent's published Zmod design. Export the bitstream and the hardware handoff: it lists every register address and interrupt line.

steps.title: Step 3: load the bitstream before anything touches it
steps.body: The Zynq FPGA manager wants a byte-swapped `.bin`, produced with `bootgen`. Load it in U-Boot, or in a vendor-style `BOOT.BIN`, or from Linux through `fpga_manager`. The driver must not probe before it is loaded.

steps.title: Step 4: the device-tree nodes
steps.body: A static node if the bitstream was loaded before Linux; an overlay if Linux loads it at runtime (the mainline kernel has no ready userspace overlay interface, so a runtime route needs more kernel work). The reference values come from the hardware handoff.

steps.title: Step 5: the driver, then user space
steps.body: Once the nodes bind, samples are read from the driver's device. That driver is the one piece nobody ships for mainline; budget the most time here.
